record.original_question: In active light-sheet microscopy for developmental biology, how can an intelligent microscope decide which measurements are actually necessary, including how, where, and when to look next, while balancing spatial resolution, temporal resolution, signal-to-noise ratio, sample health, data-processing cost, and incomplete or noisy two-dimensional image planes, in order to learn useful representations of both the biological process and the imaging process as gently as possible?

evidence.quote: Modern light-sheet microscopes can quickly generate enormous amounts of data in the range of multiple terabytes, thus predicting which measurements are actually necessary would considerably simplify the data processing pipeline or even makes it feasible in the first place.

An active microscope would be able to balance the imaging trade-offs, and learn a useful representation of the biological process while being as gentle with the specimen as possible [37]. This also involves learning a representation of the imaging process to inform the decision about how, where and when to look next for new data.

This can be achieved by separating the dynamical factors that are directly controllable (where and how to look), and those that are not (the biological process itself), learning to control what can be controlled with minimal cost, and motivating the agent to curiously explore what can not.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a light-sheet microscopy imaging system modeled as a partially observable Markov decision process in which an agent sequentially selects measurement actions a_t ∈ A at times t = 1, 2, …, where each action specifies an acquisition mode together with a spatial location and time (encoding the choice of how, where, and when to image). Each action a_t produces a (possibly incomplete, noisy) two-dimensional image plane o_t drawn from an observation distribution that depends on an unobserved latent biological state b_t evolving according to its own (uncontrolled) dynamics, and on a controllable imaging state i_t whose evolution depends on the action sequence. Each action also incurs a cost c(a_t, b_t) reflecting photodamage to the specimen, acquisition time, and data-processing load, and the achievable observation quality is governed by trade-offs among spatial resolution, temporal resolution, and signal-to-noise ratio.

Design a measurement policy π mapping observation histories to actions such that, over a finite horizon T, the policy:
(1) learns a representation φ_b of the biological process b_{1:T} and a representation φ_i of the imaging process i_{1:T}, by explicitly separating the controllable dynamical factors (where and how to look) from the uncontrolled ones (the biological process), learning to control the former with minimal cost and exploring the latter through an intrinsic curiosity-style objective;
(2) maximizes a representation-quality utility U(φ_b, φ_i) (for instance, predictive accuracy on held-out future observations or mutual information between φ_b and b_{1:T}) subject to a constraint or penalty on the cumulative cost Σ_t c(a_t, b_t).

Provide such a policy together with provable guarantees relating the achieved utility to the optimum attainable by any non-anticipative policy under the same cost budget, or prove fundamental limits on this trade-off.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is presented as an open research direction in active representation learning for intelligent microscopy. No subsequent work appears to provide a complete solution with formal guarantees; related work on event-driven and adaptive microscopy addresses pieces of the trade-off but does not resolve the joint representation-learning and acquisition-policy question.

status_evidence.title: Open Problem: Active Representation Learning
status_evidence.snippet: Posed as an open problem regarding how an active microscope should decide which measurements to acquire while balancing imaging trade-offs.
status_evidence.claim: The question is explicitly framed as an open problem.
